page.confirm.keep_on: Keep {name} on? It will not turn itself off. When what it does changes, a warning appears, a part of it fails, a continuation it sent cannot be proven to have arrived, or Codex is updated, it stays on and this page tells you; a part that fails skips only that one recovery. You can always turn it off here, from Codex or with every advanced feature at once. Its limits stay, and your administrator's policy still applies.
page.confirm.reset_credit: Use a reset credit when {window} is reached ({which}), if a recovery is waiting for usage then? A reset credit used cannot be given back.

page.confirm.send_again: Also send again when unsure? When a continuation {name} sent cannot be proven to have arrived, it is sent once more with the same marker, between 15 minutes and 6 hours later, only if neither Codex's history nor its queue holds it and nothing has happened in the conversation since. If the first one arrives after all, the conversation gets the same continuation twice. If the marker is then found twice, sending again turns itself off. This departs from 0.2, A6, E2 and H2, and works only where your administrator's policy also allows Once more when unsure.
page.confirm.send_now: Send this recovery's continuation now? Every check still runs first; it does not wait for its schedule, a postponement or the 15 minutes since the last continuation.

statement.capacity_retry.departs: A20 (at most five continuations a conversation in 24 hours, at least 15 minutes apart), A21 (the attempt, no-progress and continuation budgets), A22 (waits come only from the retry timing you chose), B9 (only a failure's kind is kept: this also reads Codex's own error code, never its words) and H2 (nothing can move a limit the product fixes).
statement.capacity_retry.does: When Codex says it is at capacity (its own error code serverOverloaded), it tries again sooner and more often than the standard edition: about a minute after the failure, then two, four and five minutes, each lengthened by up to a fifth, at least a minute apart and at most 48 times a day in one conversation. It keeps this up for as long as you choose, one to twelve hours (two by default), counted on the clock from the first failure, whatever it waited for meanwhile; after that the standard edition's own limits apply again, and they may end the task. Each try is the ordinary continuation through Codex's queue command, with its marker. Other server errors, rate limits and usage limits keep the standard edition's waits.
statement.capacity_retry.instead: The standard edition waits as its retry timing says, sends at most five continuations to a conversation in any 24 hours, at least 15 minutes apart, and stops a task after four attempts, three in a row with no progress, or six continuations.
statement.capacity_retry.risks: Retrying a busy service often adds to its load and spends your usage on continuations that may fail again, and each try is a visible message in the conversation. All advanced features together still send at most 12 times an hour; while that limit is reached, capacity errors are handled as the standard edition handles them, which may end the task. A continuation whose delivery cannot be proven is never sent again, and this feature turns itself off.
statement.capacity_retry.stop: Turn it off in the Dashboard, or turn every advanced feature off; capacity errors then wait as the standard edition makes them wait. Cancel a waiting recovery to stop that one.
statement.codex_gave_up.departs: A14 (Codex giving up without a 429 is never retried), A26 (continuation text only for a kind that is recovered) and B9 (only a failure's kind is kept, never Codex's error code and status).
statement.codex_gave_up.does: When Codex ended a turn after its own retries failed (its error code responseTooManyFailedAttempts) and the last answer it had was a server error or none at all, it continues the conversation once Codex has had time to recover: ten minutes after the failure, then 15, and at most twice a task. When the last answer was a rate limit, the standard edition already retries it. It takes up only failures from the last hour, and none from before it was turned on.
statement.codex_gave_up.instead: The standard edition retries this only when the last answer was a rate limit (429), and otherwise leaves the conversation for you.
statement.codex_gave_up.risks: Codex already tried several times, so trying again is not a fresh attempt: it may fail the same way and use your usage. A continuation whose delivery cannot be proven is never sent again, and this feature turns itself off.
statement.codex_gave_up.stop: Turn it off or set it to watch only in the Dashboard, or turn every advanced feature off; a recovery it was waiting to send then ends without being sent.
statement.compat_report.departs: B11: gh reads your GitHub sign-in, from Windows' credential storage or its own file, to make its requests; the product never sees it. C1 and C2: this edition reaches the network, through gh, where otherwise only the install script does. C3: gh is asked for GitHub addresses beyond the two lists of releases. C8: those requests are made as your GitHub account, with gh's own User-Agent. D1: the report's counts go to the project, in public. E8: a gh that has not answered in two minutes, or is still running when the Dashboard's service ends, is ended. F3: the report can be saved as a file wherever you choose. F6: gh is not one of the processes the product starts. It keeps G13: a report grants nothing and changes nothing the product does. And it keeps K5: while recovery is paused, nothing is checked or sent.
statement.compat_report.does: Writes a compatibility report from this PC's own records, as codex-compat-reporter does: counts, states and times for one Codex version, with no conversation text, id or path. You read the whole file here, with its SHA-256 and every write sending would make, and it is sent only after you type send: through gh, the GitHub CLI, signed in as you, it forks the project, adds the file on a branch and opens a public pull request. Without gh it saves the file and shows how to send it on the web.
statement.compat_report.instead: The standard edition sends nothing for a report. You write and send one with codex-compat-reporter, a separate program that reads the same records.
statement.compat_report.risks: The pull request, the fork and your GitHub login are public, and a pull request cannot be unpublished. The report's times are published to the second. A send cut off part way - the window closed, the network lost - can leave a fork or a branch behind; checking again shows what is on GitHub, and sending again is safe. Whatever gh.exe is first in a full folder on PATH is trusted to be the GitHub CLI.
statement.compat_report.stop: Turn it off here, or with All advanced features off; MCP and the icon can turn it off too. A send in progress stops before its next write when it is turned off, when recovery is paused or when an administrator's policy forbids it, and this page then shows what was already written. Nothing is ever sent unless you type send.
statement.early_reset.departs: A12 (never before the real reset time) and C9 (Codex is asked about usage only when a recovery is due).
statement.early_reset.does: While a conversation waits for a usage limit to reset, it asks Codex every five minutes whether usage is available - one question for every conversation waiting - and when two answers at least five minutes apart both say yes, it continues the waiting conversations then, before the reset time Codex gave. It only reads: it never sends anything to start a usage window or keep one open.
statement.early_reset.instead: The standard edition asks about usage only when a recovery is due, and never continues before the reset time Codex gave.
statement.early_reset.risks: Each question is a request to OpenAI through Codex. Usage that reads as available may be available for another model or plan than the one the conversation uses, and the continuation may meet the limit again; the usage check every continuation makes still applies.
statement.early_reset.stop: Turn it off in the Dashboard, or turn every advanced feature off; usage-limited conversations then wait for their reset time.
statement.goal_continuation.departs: 0.5 (the product never changes a goal's state), A2 (continuations go through one channel only, Codex's queue command), A11 (nothing is done for a conversation the app does not have open), B3 (Codex's state changes only through its queue and plugin commands) and B4 (the app server is asked only for usage and to take back a queued message).
statement.goal_continuation.does: When a usage limit paused a conversation's Codex goal, and the conversation is due to continue while the Codex app does not have it open, it sets that goal active again through Codex's own app server, so Codex carries the goal on when the app next opens the conversation. It resumes only a goal that exists and was paused by the usage limit; it never creates a goal and never reads or changes what the goal says. While the app has the conversation open, the continuation goes through Codex's queue as in the standard edition, with the goal set active first only where measurement M2b passed for your version of Codex.
statement.goal_continuation.instead: The standard edition never touches a goal. It waits until the app has the conversation open and then queues its continuation with Codex's queue command; a goal paused by the usage limit stays paused until you resume it yourself.
statement.goal_continuation.risks: Measurement M2 found that a goal set this way is not seen while the app has the conversation open, and is picked up once the app opens it again; that is why, unless measurement M2b passed for your version of Codex, it acts only on a conversation the app does not have open. Where M2b passed, it also acts on one the app has open: it sets the goal active and then queues the continuation, which M2b found carries on. Another version of Codex may handle goals differently. When the result cannot be confirmed - Codex does not answer, or the goal does not read back as resumed - that interruption is never tried again and this feature turns itself off. While a goal is carrying the conversation on, the standard continuation waits for up to ten minutes after the app opens it, so the two do not both run. Every recovery gate, limit and pause still applies.
statement.goal_continuation.stop: Turn it off in the Dashboard, or turn off every advanced feature at once; continuations then go only through Codex's queue again. A goal it already set active stays active: pause the goal in Codex if you want it to stop.
statement.long_reset_message.departs: A27 (a message a person writes is at most 2,000 characters).
statement.long_reset_message.does: Lets a message you schedule for a reset, and a message you queue, be up to 8,154 characters - the most one continuation can carry - instead of 2,000.
statement.long_reset_message.instead: A message you write, like the Custom message, is at most 2,000 characters.
statement.long_reset_message.risks: A long message uses more of the window it starts than a short one. Turned off, every waiting message longer than 2,000 characters - at a reset or in the queue - is cancelled.
statement.long_reset_message.stop: Turn it off here or with All advanced features off; waiting messages over 2,000 characters, at a reset or in the queue, are then cancelled.
statement.marker_free_continuation.depar: A2 (continuations go through one channel only, Codex's queue command), A4 (each continuation carries its marker, and it counts as delivered only when that marker is found), B3 (Codex's state changes only through its queue and plugin commands) and B4 (the app server is asked only for usage and to take back a queued message).
statement.marker_free_continuation.does: Sends each continuation without the marker the standard edition ends it with. The message is added to the conversation's queue through Codex's own app server, under an id made from the interruption, and that id - which Codex keeps on the message - is what proves it arrived. Past its daily limits, a continuation goes with the marker, as in the standard edition.
statement.marker_free_continuation.inste: The standard edition sends every continuation through Codex's queue command and ends it with a short marker, [codex-auto-resume:…], which is how it finds its own message in the conversation afterwards.
statement.marker_free_continuation.risks: It rests on an app-server request measured on one version of Codex (M7); another version may refuse it or stop keeping the id. When arrival cannot be proven - the app server refuses or does not answer, or the message never shows - the continuation is treated as uncertain, exactly as the standard edition treats one: it is never sent again, and this feature turns itself off. Every recovery gate and limit stays as it is.
statement.marker_free_continuation.stop: Turn it off in the Dashboard, or turn off every advanced feature at once; continuations then go through Codex's queue command with the marker again. One already sent without a marker is still followed by its id to the end.
statement.once_more_when_unsure.departs: 0.2 (it never sends again when the first continuation may already have been delivered), A6 (an uncertain delivery is never sent again), E2 (better to miss a resume than resume twice) and H2 (nothing can resend an uncertain submission).
statement.once_more_when_unsure.does: When it cannot be proven that a continuation arrived, sends it once more, its words built the same way and with the same marker, if between 15 minutes and 6 hours after the first: Codex was never seen holding it in its queue, neither Codex's history nor its queue holds the marker, Codex's history was current at every look since, the conversation has no later turn and nothing queued, its attempts are not used up, and every check a send passes still holds. A continuation is sent again at most once, and one that Pause or Observe only takes back is not sent again.
statement.once_more_when_unsure.instead: The standard edition never sends a continuation again once its delivery is uncertain. It follows it for 24 hours in case it arrives, and otherwise leaves it as uncertain.
statement.once_more_when_unsure.risks: If the first continuation did arrive late, the conversation gets the same continuation twice and Codex may do the same work twice; if the marker is then found twice, it turns itself off. The words are built again from your settings as they are then. After the watcher restarts it cannot prove the history stayed current, and sends nothing again.
statement.once_more_when_unsure.stop: Turn it off here, from Codex, or turn off every advanced feature at once. An uncertain continuation is then only followed, as in the standard edition.
statement.reset_credit.departs: A12 (a look before the real reset time, once a credit reset the window), B3 (it changes your account: a credit is spent), B4 (it asks the app server account/rateLimitResetCredit/consume), B10 (it keeps how many credits you have and when the soonest expires), C4 (it reads usage and spends on its own, at the time you chose) and C9 (it reads usage when no recovery is due).
statement.reset_credit.does: Lets you pick a usage limit - the next 5-hour limit, a later one, or the weekly limit - and when it is reached while a recovery waits for usage, uses one of your reset credits so the recovery can go on. While a rule waits it reads usage every 15 minutes and counts each window's resets and fills itself. Before it spends one it reads usage again: the window must still be full, and how many credits you have and when they expire must both be readable. Until measurement MR has passed on this Codex it never spends on its own - you press Use a reset credit now - and after that only if you did not choose Ask me first.
statement.reset_credit.instead: The standard edition never spends a reset credit and never reads how many you have: a recovery waits until the limit resets, and usage is read only when a recovery is due. You can still spend a credit yourself in Codex's /usage.
statement.reset_credit.risks: A credit spent cannot be given back, and one may be spent shortly before the window would have reset anyway. If you redeem two credits yourself inside one window, the count can run one window late. It never spends more than one credit for one filling of a window, two in a day or seven in a week; never while recovery is paused, in Observe only, in quiet hours or with no recovery waiting; and never when the count or the expiry cannot be read. A spend whose result cannot be known turns it off.
statement.reset_credit.stop: Turn it off on this page, or turn every advanced feature off, or cancel a rule here or in Pending. A spend already asked of Codex cannot be taken back.
statement.reset_message.departs: A8 (its message passes the checks that apply to it; a recovery's budgets and failure checks are not run), A17 (a turn after it does not take it back), A26 (the words are yours, not a template, and recover no failure), C4 (it sends at a time you chose), C9 (it reads usage when no recovery is due), D2 (your words are kept until they are sent), H4 (a Pause takes back a message Codex already holds and cancels it, rather than returning it to waiting) and H6 (Cancel no longer reaches a message being sent).
statement.reset_message.does: Lets you write a message of your own for one conversation that is switched on, and pick when it goes: when the next 5-hour limit resets, a later reset, or the weekly one. At that reset the watcher sends it once, exactly as you wrote it, with its marker after a blank line, through every check a continuation passes - the conversation open in the app, nothing else queued there, usage available - and in place of a continuation waiting there for the same reset. While a message waits it reads usage every 15 minutes to count the resets. Up to 2,000 characters, one message to a conversation and ten in all.
statement.reset_message.instead: The standard edition sends only its own continuation, from its templates or your Custom message, and only to recover a failed turn: it never sends at a time you choose, and reads usage only when a recovery is due.
statement.reset_message.risks: Your message may arrive when you no longer want it: it goes as written, whatever the conversation has become. If you redeem two credits yourself inside one window, it can go one window late. If this PC is off or recovery is paused for longer than the window, it waits for you to say go on. It is never sent twice; one that cannot be proven to have arrived a day after it was sent turns this off.
statement.reset_message.stop: Cancel it here or in Pending before it is sent, switch its conversation off, or turn this off - its words are deleted. Once it is being sent, Cancel no longer reaches it.
statement.send_now.departs: A8 (the claim checks the schedule and the budgets again, passing none), A20 (at least 15 minutes between two continuations in a conversation), A21 (the attempt budget stops a recovery) and H2 (nothing can force a send).
statement.send_now.does: Adds Send now to this page while it is on. For one waiting recovery you choose, the watcher sends its continuation at its next look instead of when its schedule says: it passes the wait before the next try, a postponement, the minutes before a first send, the 15 minutes between two continuations in one conversation and an attempt budget you set that is used up, but never one your administrator set. Every other check still runs, and a request not used within 15 minutes lapses.
statement.send_now.instead: The standard edition sends a continuation only when its schedule says, at least 15 minutes after the last one in the same conversation, and never past the attempt budget. Retry now only brings the next check forward and skips nothing.
statement.send_now.risks: A continuation sent sooner may meet the same failure again and use an attempt the schedule would have kept for later. It never sends before a usage limit resets, in quiet hours, past an attempt limit your administrator set, past five continuations in a conversation in a day, while recovery is paused or the conversation is off, before the app has the conversation open, while something else is queued for it, or without usage.
statement.send_now.stop: Turn it off here or turn off every advanced feature at once; a request not yet used is then never used, even if you turn it on again, and the recovery waits for its schedule.
statement.sign_in_retry.departs: 0.5 (sign-in failures are never retried), A14 (401 and 403 are never retried) and A26 (continuation text only for a kind that is recovered).
statement.sign_in_retry.does: When a turn fails because Codex was not signed in (its error code unauthorized, or status 401), it waits at least ten minutes and continues the conversation once, and only when the usage read every continuation already needs shows Codex is signed in again. Once a task and twice a day in all; if the continuation fails at sign-in again, it stops there, and after a day without a working usage read it gives up. It never reads or changes Codex's sign-in, its auth.json or any token, and never asks Codex to sign in or out. A permission refusal (403) is never retried. It takes up only failures from the last hour, and none from before it was turned on.
statement.sign_in_retry.instead: The standard edition never retries a sign-in failure: you sign in again in Codex and continue yourself.
statement.sign_in_retry.risks: A usage read proves Codex reaches your account, not that every request will be accepted, so the continuation may fail again. If you signed in with another account, the conversation continues under that one.
statement.sign_in_retry.stop: Turn it off or set it to watch only in the Dashboard, or turn every advanced feature off; a recovery it was waiting to send then ends without being sent.
statement.start_with_codex.departs: C4 (the product starts nothing on its own when Codex starts) and F6 (it adds one process-creation route, through WMI, beyond the ones the standard edition uses).
statement.start_with_codex.does: Starts the watcher when Codex starts, even inside the job Codex closes when it quits. With this on and no watcher running, it asks Windows (WMI) to start the watcher outside that job, so it keeps running after Codex closes. It registers nothing.
statement.start_with_codex.instead: The standard edition starts nothing here: where Codex would end the watcher it writes one line to say so and waits for you to start the watcher yourself once Codex has closed.
statement.start_with_codex.risks: Its only purpose is to leave a limit Codex places on its plugins on purpose. If WMI is off, or a policy blocks process creation through it, nothing starts and the reason is logged; you are never asked to change that policy. It starts the watcher and nothing else, keeps every recovery gate, and never starts a second copy.
statement.start_with_codex.stop: Turn it off in the Dashboard, or turn off every advanced feature at once. It never starts a second watcher while one is running, and it only ever starts this installation's own launcher.
statement.structured_rules.departs: 0.5 (unknown failures are never retried), A13 (only the classified kinds are recovered), A14 (anything unclassified is never retried), A26 (continuation text only for a kind that is recovered), B9 (only a failure's kind is kept, never Codex's error code) and H2 (nothing can retry an unknown failure).
statement.structured_rules.does: Lets you write up to ten rules in the Dashboard. Each names one of Codex's own error codes, and if you like a range of status numbers, and the kind of temporary failure to treat it as: a dropped connection, a timeout, a rate limit, a server error or a broken stream. A rule applies only to a failure the product could not classify; it then waits as that kind waits in your retry timing, counts against that kind's budget and follows that kind's switch in Settings. A code the product already knows can never be a rule, nor one whose name speaks of a policy, budget, quota, permission, approval, sign-in or cancellation, and no rule makes a failure a usage limit. Rules read codes, never the words of an error. It takes up only failures from the last hour, and none from before it was turned on.
statement.structured_rules.instead: The standard edition never retries a failure it cannot classify, and nothing you set can change that.
statement.structured_rules.risks: A rule is your judgement that a code is temporary. A wrong one retries failures that retrying cannot fix, until that kind's budget runs out, and Codex may rename or reuse a code in another version. The continuation is the short standard message.
statement.structured_rules.stop: Remove the rule, turn the feature off or set it to watch only in the Dashboard, or turn every advanced feature off. A recovery a rule took up and has not sent then ends without being sent.
statement.unknown_failure_budget.departs: 0.5 (unknown failures are never retried), A13 (only the classified kinds are recovered), A14 (anything unclassified is never retried), A26 (continuation text only for a kind that is recovered), B9 (only a failure's kind is kept, never Codex's error code), D2 (state holds only the product's own fixed words, never a code Codex chose) and H2 (nothing can retry an unknown failure).
statement.unknown_failure_budget.does: When a turn fails with an error code of Codex's that the product cannot classify, it continues the conversation anyway, on a budget of its own: one to three tries a task, as you choose (one by default), at most three a day in one conversation, the first ten minutes after the failure, then 15 and 30. It never takes up a failure that came with no code, or a code whose name speaks of a policy, budget, quota, permission, approval, sign-in or cancellation. Each failure it takes up leaves a sample on this PC: Codex's error code, the status number, how many items of each kind the turn left, when it failed and how long it ran - never a word of the error, the conversation or the reply. You see the samples here, and a diagnostics export you ask for includes them; nothing sends them. It takes up only failures from the last hour, and none from before it was turned on.
statement.unknown_failure_budget.instead: The standard edition never retries a failure it cannot classify: the conversation waits for you.
statement.unknown_failure_budget.risks: A failure nobody classified may be one retrying cannot help, or one where trying again repeats something a person should have decided; Codex continues from the short standard message. A sample keeps an error code Codex chose, which may say more than the product's own words. A continuation whose delivery cannot be proven is never sent again, and this feature turns itself off.
statement.unknown_failure_budget.stop: Turn it off or set it to watch only in the Dashboard, or turn every advanced feature off; a recovery it was waiting to send then ends without being sent. Samples are kept 90 days at most.
warning.compat_unknown: It is not known whether what it relies on works with this version of Codex.
warning.engine_unknown: The version of Codex is not known yet. If you turn it on, it turns off again once the version is known, so that you can confirm that version.
warning.failed_here: A compatibility check of what it relies on failed on this computer.
warning.incompatible: The compatibility data says what it relies on does not work with this version of Codex.
warning.local_check_failed: A check on this computer found that this version of Codex lacks what it relies on.
warning.measurement_failed: A measurement of what it relies on failed. It may not work with your Codex.
warning.note: None of these stops you turning it on. Turning it on confirms you have read them, and if a new problem appears later, it turns itself off.
warning.title: Warnings
warning.unmeasured: What it relies on has not been measured with this version of Codex.
statement.parallel_dispatch.does: Lets the watcher wait for Codex to take two to four continuations at once, each in a conversation of its own, instead of one after another. Every check, every claim and the last look before each send still run one at a time; only the wait for Codex's answer to each send overlaps. You choose how many at once (2 by default); until this has been measured on the Codex you have (MQ), never more than 2. One conversation still never has two continuations on their way.
statement.parallel_dispatch.departs: 0.5 (one recovery is dispatched at a time) and A19 (continuations are dispatched in sequence, under one lock).
statement.parallel_dispatch.instead: The standard edition sends one continuation at a time and waits for Codex's answer, up to 45 seconds, before it looks at the next one.
statement.parallel_dispatch.risks: Several Codex queue processes start close together, which a busy or slow Codex may answer late or not at all. A continuation whose delivery cannot be proven is never sent again, and this feature turns itself off.
statement.parallel_dispatch.stop: Turn it off here or turn every advanced feature off; from the next look every continuation is sent one at a time again.
page.watchlog.answer.queue_for_open: Queued it for when the conversation is opened
page.watchlog.answer.to_session: Queued it for the other Codex session that has the conversation
page.watchlog.answer.silent: Started the turn with no words
page.watchlog.answer.records: A message of yours it would have sent
name.queue_for_open: Queue for when a conversation is opened
statement.queue_for_open.does: When a usage limit has reset in a conversation the Codex app does not have open, sends the ordinary continuation anyway and leaves it in Codex's queue, so Codex runs it when you open that conversation. It stays queued for the days you choose (3 by default, 7 at most) and is taken back after that. Each interruption is queued this way once; once taken back, it waits for the app as usual. Measured on codex-cli 0.158 (M1); on another version of Codex it is unmeasured.
statement.queue_for_open.departs: A11 (nothing is queued on the off chance that a conversation will be opened). It keeps A17, H4 and H6: every withdrawal still happens at once.
statement.queue_for_open.instead: The standard edition waits until the Codex app has the conversation open before it sends anything there.
statement.queue_for_open.risks: A message may wait in Codex for days, and while it waits its recovery counts as open, so an action set for after every recovery has finished waits too. If Codex does not run it within three minutes of the conversation being opened, it is taken back, sent the ordinary way, and this feature turns itself off.
statement.queue_for_open.stop: Turn it off here or turn every advanced feature off; at its next look a queued message is taken back out of Codex's queue and waits for the app as usual.
page.tripped.not_delivered_on_open: Turned off: a conversation was opened and Codex did not run the message queued for it.
page.kept.not_delivered_on_open: It stayed on although Codex did not run a message queued for a conversation when it was opened.
name.empty_response: Continue a turn that ended with no reply
statement.empty_response.does: When a turn in a conversation of yours ended with no reply - only your message and Codex's reasoning in it, which is all it judges by, never the words - sends one short continuation of its own: "The last turn ended without a reply. Please continue from where you stopped." It looks twice, half a minute apart, before it decides, and leaves alone a conversation whose goal Codex is keeping going or has stopped. Each such turn is answered once, and a run of them twice at most. Until this has been measured on the Codex you have (ME), it says so.
statement.empty_response.departs: 0.5 (only failed turns are recovered), A13 (only failures the product can classify) and A26 (the product's continuations are its fixed templates or your Custom message).
statement.empty_response.instead: The standard edition leaves a turn Codex completed alone, with or without a reply.
statement.empty_response.risks: Codex may have meant to end the turn quietly, and the continuation starts work you did not ask for. It is sent only while that turn is still the conversation's latest, and never twice for one turn.
statement.empty_response.stop: Turn it off here or turn every advanced feature off; a continuation not yet sent is dropped at once.
continue.empty_response: The last turn ended without a reply. Please continue from where you stopped.
name.subagent_parent: Tell a parent which of its subagents stopped
statement.subagent_parent.does: When a subagent of one of your conversations stops on a failure, the parent conversation is told in fixed words, one line for each subagent, five at most: "Subagent <its id> stopped: <why>. Resume or respawn it only if it is still needed." If the parent failed too, the lines are added to the continuation the product sends it anyway. If the parent finished normally, it is sent one continuation with the lines - only once this has been measured on the Codex you have (MS). Nothing is ever written to a subagent, and each stop is told once.
statement.subagent_parent.departs: 0.5 (only failed turns are recovered), A15 (subagent conversations are never detected or recovered) and A26 (the product's continuations are its fixed templates or your Custom message).
statement.subagent_parent.instead: The standard edition does not look at subagents at all; a parent that failed is sent the ordinary continuation.
statement.subagent_parent.risks: The parent may resume or respawn work you meant to drop. Only a subagent's id and a fixed word for why it stopped are told - never anything it said.
statement.subagent_parent.stop: Turn it off here or turn every advanced feature off; a continuation not yet sent is dropped at once.
continue.subagent.line: Subagent {child} stopped: {kind}. Resume or respawn it only if it is still needed.
statement.keep_going.does: For a conversation you pick in the Dashboard, with a count of 1 to 10: when its latest turn ended well and it has been idle for a minute, sends one continuation of its own - "Carry on with the next step of the plan." - up to the count you chose. It stops when a turn made no progress, when every step of the plan is completed, when a goal of Codex's own is keeping it going, when a turn failed or was interrupted, or when the count is used. It reads only the kinds of item a turn left and the status of each plan step, never their words. Until this has been measured on the Codex you have (MK), no more than 3 are sent.
statement.keep_going.departs: A13 (only failures are recovered), A26 (the product's continuations are its fixed templates or your Custom message) and B9 (nothing is read from the content of a conversation's items).
statement.keep_going.instead: The standard edition leaves a turn Codex completed alone; Codex's own goals (/goal) keep a conversation going within Codex's own limits.
statement.keep_going.risks: Work goes on when you might have wanted it to stop: stop it in the Dashboard, or switch the conversation off. It is paced like every recovery, fifteen minutes apart and five a day in one conversation.
statement.keep_going.stop: Turn it off here or turn every advanced feature off; no conversation is kept going any more, and a continuation not yet sent is dropped.
continue.keep_going: Carry on with the next step of the plan.
statement.prompt_queue.does: Lets you queue messages of your own for one conversation in the Dashboard: to go after the turn now running, at a time you pick, or every day or week from a time - 30 times and 30 days at most. They go in the order you queued them, each once, exactly as you wrote them, and one can wait for the one before it to arrive. They are paced like every recovery: fifteen minutes apart and five a day in one conversation. Your words leave this PC once a message is sent. Codex's own automations are the official way to schedule work; these wait for usage and go to one exact conversation. Until this has been measured on the Codex you have (MT), "after this turn" says it is unproven.
statement.prompt_queue.departs: A8 (its messages pass the checks that apply to them; a recovery's budgets and failure checks are not run), A17 (a turn after one does not take it back), A26 (the words are yours, not a template, and recover no failure), A27 (a message may be longer than 2,000 characters while Longer messages is on), C4 (they go at times you chose, and on a schedule), D2 (your words are kept until they are sent), H4 (a Pause takes back a message Codex already holds and holds it for you to go on or cancel, rather than returning it to waiting) and H6 (Cancel no longer reaches a message being sent).
statement.prompt_queue.instead: The standard edition sends nothing of yours but the Custom message, and only to recover a failure.
statement.prompt_queue.risks: A queued message can go when you no longer want it: cancel it in the Dashboard. One Codex already holds is taken back out of its queue; if Codex will not give it back, its row says so and it is never sent again. A message queued for after this turn waits in Codex's queue until that turn ends.
statement.prompt_queue.stop: Turn it off here or turn every advanced feature off; every queued message Codex does not hold yet is cancelled, its words with it.
page.keep.title: Conversations kept going
page.keep.capped: Until this has been measured on this Codex, no more than {n} are sent.
page.confirm.keep_going: Keep {conversation} going for up to {n} continuations? Each is sent after a turn that ended well, and it stops on no progress, a finished plan or an active goal.
page.done.keep_going: It keeps going from its next finished turn.
page.refused.keep_count_invalid: That number is not one on offer. Nothing was changed.
page.queue.title: Queued messages
page.queue.depends: Wait for the one before it to arrive
page.queue.state.held: held for you: go on or cancel
page.queue.state.in_codex: queued in Codex - Cancel takes it back
page.queue.state.refused: Codex would not give it back; it is never sent again
page.queue.unproven: After this turn is unproven on this Codex until it has been measured.
page.confirm.prompt: Queue this message for {conversation}, {when}? It is sent once, exactly as written.
page.refused.prompt_refused: That message cannot be queued: it is empty or too long, holds a marker of this product's, or is one of its own continuations.
page.refused.queue_full: As many messages are queued as may: five for a conversation, twenty in all. Cancel one to queue another.
page.refused.dependency_unknown: No message is queued before it in that conversation, so it cannot wait for one.
page.wording.help: Your words may hold {percent}, {window}, {stop_at} and {reset}, each filled in when they are sent, and nothing else in braces. A window with no words of its own is sent the standard wording.
page.wording.wrap_custom_five_hour: Your words for the five-hour window
page.wording.wrap_custom_weekly: Your words for the weekly window
page.done.wording: {name} uses these words from now on.
page.refused.wording.empty: The words cannot be empty. To use the standard wording for this window, leave the box empty and save.
page.refused.wording.too_long: The words are longer than a custom message may be. Nothing was changed.
page.refused.wording.control: The words hold a control character. Nothing was changed.
page.refused.wording.marker: The words hold a marker of this product's own. Nothing was changed.
page.refused.wording.placeholder: Only {percent}, {window}, {stop_at} and {reset} may be in braces. Nothing was changed.
page.preview.title: What is sent, exactly
page.preview.300: When the five-hour window reaches it:
page.preview.10080: When the weekly window reaches it:
page.option.no_window: Both windows are switched off, so this feature acts on neither of them.
page.refused.option_order: For each window, the warning must be at or below the wrap-up, and the wrap-up below the stop its words ask for. Nothing was changed.
page.warn.stop_before_words: Saved. The forced stop is below the stop the wrap-up's words ask for, so it may stop Codex before Codex stops itself.
statement.usage_meter.does: While the Codex app runs, reads your Codex usage on its own every few minutes - 5 to 60, as you choose or type in, 15 by default - and shows it in the icon's tooltip and in the popup. When a window reaches the percentage you set for a warning (85% by default, each window its own, any whole number you type in), it shows a notice, once for that window. Each window - the five-hour and the weekly - can be switched off on its own: it is still read and shown, and no notice warns of it. Wrap up near a limit and Stop near a limit each have their own switch for each window. The reading is only shown: whether a recovery may go is still decided by the reading the product makes when a recovery is due.
statement.usage_meter.instead: The standard edition reads usage only when a recovery is due, and the popup shows the last such reading; nothing is read on a schedule.
statement.usage_meter.departs: C4 (nothing happens on its own, on a schedule) and C9 (usage is read only when a recovery is due).
statement.usage_meter.risks: Each reading is one short request to Codex's own app server, as a recovery's is; reading often adds a little to what Codex does. Codex may change how it reports usage: a reading that cannot be read is shown as nothing and warns of nothing. Until MU has been measured on the Codex you have, its readings rest on an earlier measurement.
statement.usage_meter.stop: Turn it off here or turn every advanced feature off: nothing more is read on a schedule, and Wrap up near a limit and Stop near a limit, which need it, turn off with it.
statement.usage_wrap_up.does: When a window you let it act on reaches the wrap-up percentage you set (90% by default, each window its own), each conversation that is switched on and has a turn running is sent one message, once for that window - in the wording you pick: short, standard, detailed, with the numbers ("You have used 90% of the five-hour limit. Get ready to stop safely, and stop when it reaches 95%." - the stop it asks for is its own number, apart from Stop near a limit's), or your own words for each window. Include the reset time adds when that window resets. The page shows the exact words under your choice. It goes through Codex's queue as every continuation does, so Codex delivers it when the current turn ends. With Continue after the reset (on by default), a conversation that then ended well is sent one continuation once the window resets. It needs the usage meter, which is turned on with it.
statement.usage_wrap_up.instead: The standard edition sends nothing until a turn fails; a turn runs on until Codex stops it at the limit.
statement.usage_wrap_up.departs: A13 (only failures are recovered) and A26 (the product's continuations are its fixed templates or your Custom message, for a failure it recovers).
statement.usage_wrap_up.risks: The message arrives only when the current turn ends, which may be after the limit is reached: it cannot stop a turn midway (Stop near a limit can). A turn that ended before the message went gets none. Your own words are sent as you wrote them, with only the numbers filled in. The continuation after the reset goes only if nothing newer happened in the conversation. It is paced like every recovery: fifteen minutes apart and five a day in one conversation, and two a day of these.
statement.usage_wrap_up.stop: Turn it off here, turn the usage meter off, or turn every advanced feature off; a message not yet sent is dropped.
statement.usage_pause.does: When a window you let it act on reaches the stop percentage you set (97% by default, each window its own), each conversation that is switched on and has a turn running is stopped, as the Stop button in the Codex app stops one - through the app's own internal channel, once for that window - and the product sends no further continuation until the window resets. This works only for a conversation the Codex app has open; where it cannot stop a turn, the product only holds its continuations and a notice says so. Codex pauses a stopped conversation's queue until the turn started after the reset lets it go; with Continue after the reset off, a notice asks you to press Resume in Codex. When the window resets, a conversation it stopped is continued once (Continue after the reset, a choice of Wrap up near a limit, on by default) by a turn started through the same channel, only if nothing newer happened there and the app has it open. Messages you queued yourself, and anything you type in Codex, are not touched. It needs the usage meter, which is turned on with it.
statement.usage_pause.instead: The standard edition never stops a running turn: it goes on sending recoveries until the limit itself is reached, and then waits for the reset.
statement.usage_pause.departs: A2 (one channel only, codex queue): its continuation after the reset is a turn started through the Codex app's internal channel; B3 (Codex's state changes only through official interfaces): it stops a turn through that channel; C9 (usage is read only when a recovery is due): it decides on the usage meter's reading; and H6 (a running turn is never stopped): stopping one is what it does.
statement.usage_pause.risks: A stopped turn may leave work half done; the wrap-up's words ask Codex to stop safely first. The app's internal channel is not a documented interface: a new Codex app may change it, and then nothing is stopped - the product only holds, and says so. Codex keeps a stopped conversation's queue paused, even across a restart, until you press Resume. Work may wait that could still have run in the usage left, and a reading that is old or wrong may stop a turn or hold recoveries too early.
statement.usage_pause.stop: Turn it off here, turn the usage meter off, or turn every advanced feature off: no turn is stopped any more, whatever was held goes on as it would have, and a continuation after the reset not yet started is dropped.
continue.wrap_up.standard: Please finish the current step, then stop.
continue.wrap_up.detailed: Commit what is pending, write down where you are and what is left, then stop.
continue.wrap_up.numbers: You have used {percent}% of {window}. Get ready to stop safely, and stop when it reaches {stop_at}%.
continue.after_reset: The usage limit has reset. Check where you stopped and continue.
page.confirm.requires: It needs {names}, so turning it on turns that on too. What each one does is below; this one yes turns them all on.
page.done.on_with: {name} is on, and so is what it needs: {names}.
page.done.also_off: {names} turned off first, because it needs {name}. Then {name} turned off.
page.refused.requirement: What this feature needs could not be turned on with it, so nothing was turned on. Try again in a moment.
page.refused.requirement_failed_here: A feature this one needs failed a compatibility check on this computer, so neither was turned on.
page.refused.failed_here: A compatibility check of what it relies on failed on this computer, so it cannot be kept on. You can still turn it on.
page.tripped.requirement_off: Turned off: a feature it needs is no longer on.
page.kept.requirement_off: It stayed on although a feature it needs is no longer on.
name.every_conversation: Recover every conversation but Codex's own
statement.every_conversation.does: Takes up a failed turn in every conversation of the Codex app except the ones Codex makes for itself: subagents (Tell a parent which of its subagents stopped handles those), reviews (guardian_review), memory passes (memory_consolidation) and conversations an agent created (agent_created_thread). A conversation with a label Codex adds later is taken up too, instead of left alone. Archived conversations, those of another Codex home, and those of a terminal or VS Code are still never taken up.
statement.every_conversation.instead: The standard edition takes up only conversations it can prove are your own: those Codex labels as yours, those handed over from ChatGPT, and those with no label at all.
statement.every_conversation.departs: A15 (only the desktop app's own user conversations are detected).
statement.every_conversation.risks: A conversation Codex uses for itself under a new label could be continued, which may cost usage or add a message where none was wanted. Every recovery gate still applies: the conversation must be switched on and open in the app before anything is sent.
statement.every_conversation.stop: Turn it off here or turn every advanced feature off; only your own conversations are taken up again, and a recovery already waiting in any other is not sent.
name.headless_run: Run a conversation here while Codex is closed
statement.headless_run.does: When a recovery is due in a conversation that nothing has open - the Codex app is closed and no terminal or VS Code session holds it - runs that one turn here, on Codex's own app server, with the continuation the standard edition would send and the settings Codex saved for that conversation. Every approval the turn asks for is declined: open the conversation in Codex to approve. The turn runs for the hours you choose at most (1 by default, 6 at most) and is stopped at once when the Codex app starts.
statement.headless_run.instead: The standard edition waits until the Codex app has the conversation open, and sends nothing until then.
statement.headless_run.departs: 0.5 (it wakes a conversation through thread/resume and runs a turn of its own), A2 (a way to Codex beside codex queue), A11 (something is done for a conversation the app does not hold), B3 and B4 (more of Codex's app server: thread/resume, turn/start, turn/interrupt and thread/unsubscribe), E8 and F8 (a Codex helper process that lives for the turn, which this ends). It keeps A4: the continuation carries its marker, and its arrival is proven by it.
statement.headless_run.risks: Work is done while nobody watches, within the conversation's own saved permissions: a command those settings allow can run. A conversation saved with full access, with an outside sandbox or with approvals that go to anyone but you is refused before anything starts. While the turn runs, the conversation is busy for Codex. That a turn on a conversation's own settings behaves (M6B) has not been measured on every Codex version.
statement.headless_run.stop: Turn it off here or turn every advanced feature off; a turn already running then ends at its cap. Press Stop... beside it under Turns run here now, on this page, to interrupt it now; starting the Codex app interrupts it too.
name.other_sessions: Recover CLI, TUI and VS Code conversations
statement.other_sessions.does: Also finds the failures of conversations you run in a terminal (the Codex CLI and TUI) or in the VS Code extension, and recovers them as it recovers the Codex app's: while another Codex session holds such a conversation, the continuation goes through codex queue for that session to take; if that session ends first, the continuation is taken back and waits again. With Run a conversation here while Codex is closed also on, one nothing holds is run here.
statement.other_sessions.instead: The standard edition looks only at the Codex app's own conversations, and waits with its own reason while another Codex session holds one.
statement.other_sessions.departs: A15 (only the desktop app's conversations are detected), A11 (it sends while a Codex session other than the app holds the conversation) and B6 (it reads from such a conversation's first line which Codex version wrote it, and waits while that is newer than the Codex here). It keeps A2, A3, A4, A17, H4 and H6: one channel, the exact conversation, the marker, newer work wins, and Pause and Cancel take a queued continuation back.
statement.other_sessions.risks: The words Codex uses to tell these conversations apart (MO) have not been measured on every Codex version: a wrong word finds nothing, never the wrong conversation. A session that ends with the continuation still queued leaves it to be taken back, and one that cannot be is never sent twice.
statement.other_sessions.stop: Turn it off here or turn every advanced feature off; the waiting recoveries of those conversations are then cancelled, and one already sent is followed to its end.
page.tripped.not_dispatched_by_session: Turned off: a terminal or VS Code session did not take a message queued for it in time.
page.kept.not_dispatched_by_session: It stayed on although a terminal or VS Code session did not take a message queued for it in time.
name.compact_continue: Compact a full conversation, then continue
statement.compact_continue.does: When a turn fails because the conversation is longer than its model's context window, it is compacted and then continued once. If the Codex app has the conversation open, the recovery waits - its row in Pending says "Run /compact in Codex; it continues after" - until you run /compact in Codex yourself; once you have, the ordinary continuation follows. If nothing has it open and Codex is closed, it is compacted here on Codex's own app server (thread/compact/start), then continued here as Run a conversation here while Codex is closed would. Codex's own automatic compaction comes first; this is for when it did not.
statement.compact_continue.instead: The standard edition never retries a full context window: it tells you the conversation is too long and to compact it or start a new one.
statement.compact_continue.departs: 0.5 (a turn of its own, through thread/resume), A2, A11, B3, B4, E8 and F8 (as Run a conversation here while Codex is closed), A13 and A14 (a context-length failure is taken up), A16 (the continuation follows the compaction turn, so the failure is no longer the latest turn), A17 (a compaction turn does not supersede it) and A26 (the continuation's words for a failure the standard edition does not recover).
statement.compact_continue.risks: A compaction loses detail of the earlier conversation. If the compaction fails or does not end within ten minutes, or none comes within a day, the recovery ends as the failure it is. That compaction behaves here (MX) and after your /compact (MXA) has not been measured on every Codex version.
statement.compact_continue.stop: Turn it off here or turn every advanced feature off; a full conversation then ends as the standard edition ends it.
name.model_fallback: Use Codex's default model when one is at capacity
statement.model_fallback.does: When a turn keeps failing because its model is at capacity, for as many attempts as you choose (2 by default), and nothing has the conversation open while Codex is closed, runs the next turn here on Codex's default model instead, then puts the conversation's own model back. Only where the conversation is on another model than the default; never for a usage, rate, sign-in or billing failure.
statement.model_fallback.instead: The standard edition retries the same model, at its own pace, and never changes a conversation's model.
statement.model_fallback.departs: 0.5 (it changes and replays a model setting, and runs a turn of its own), A2, A11, B3, B4, E8 and F8 (as Run a conversation here while Codex is closed) and B9 (it reads Codex's error code, not only a kind).
statement.model_fallback.risks: The turn runs on another model, which may answer differently. If Codex refuses to put the conversation's model back, Pending and History say so, and you switch it back in Codex. Which way puts it back (MF) has not been measured on every Codex version.
statement.model_fallback.stop: Turn it off here or turn every advanced feature off; the next recovery then stays on the conversation's own model.
statement.silent_continuation.does: When a conversation is run here while Codex is closed, its continuation is started with no words at all, so nothing extra appears in the conversation; its arrival is proven by the id it was started under. It continues nothing by itself: it changes only how Run a conversation here while Codex is closed, or a compacted conversation's continuation, starts its turn.
statement.silent_continuation.instead: The standard edition always sends a short sentence with a marker at its end, which shows in the conversation.
statement.silent_continuation.departs: A4 (no marker: the turn is proven by its id) and A26 (no words at all).
statement.silent_continuation.risks: Whether Codex starts a turn with no words, and keeps its id (M3B), has not been measured on every Codex version. Where Codex refuses it, that turn is started with the usual words instead, and this stops answering for that Codex version.
statement.silent_continuation.stop: Turn it off here or turn every advanced feature off; continuations then carry their words and marker again.
page.tripped.refused_by_codex: Turned off: Codex refused to start a turn with no words.
page.kept.refused_by_codex: It stayed on although Codex refused to start a turn with no words.
page.runs.title: Turns run here now
page.confirm.run_stop: Stop this turn? Codex interrupts it at the watcher's next look, as Stop in Codex would, and the recovery ends as that turn ends.
page.done.run_stop: Asked. The watcher stops the turn at its next look.
page.row.compact: Run /compact in Codex; it continues after
page.row.model_not_restored: This conversation now uses another model; switch it back in Codex
page.row.silent: continued with no words, proven by its id
page.keep_on.never: It cannot be kept on: turning itself off when something goes wrong is what keeps it safe.
